name: Refined baseline
why: The closest direction to the current app: familiar proportions and a small status dot.
tradeoff: The project stays in the body, so a long workspace name competes with the message.

name: Graphite quiet
why: A calm, text-only card. No icon, badge, or extra metadata is needed to read it.
tradeoff: Completion and attention rely on the wording rather than an additional visual marker.

name: Ink frame
why: A precise outline and divider make the card easy to distinguish from a dark editor.
tradeoff: The stronger frame is more visible than the other dark options.

name: Slate metadata
why: A small project line gives the title and the message their own space.
tradeoff: An extra text row makes this one slightly taller.

name: Charcoal ring
why: An outlined status symbol is easy to spot without a filled icon tile.
tradeoff: The icon column leaves less horizontal room for the message.

name: Obsidian hairline
why: A thin top accent gives a nearly black card a restrained identity.
tradeoff: The edge treatment is more decorative than a simple dot.

name: Porcelain
why: A crisp light counterpart to the refined baseline, with the same reading order.
tradeoff: A white card attracts more attention over a very dark desktop.

name: Paper rule
why: Straightforward typography and a fine separator give it an editorial feel.
tradeoff: The divider creates a more formal, document-like appearance.

name: Warm stone
why: A warm neutral surface avoids the glare of pure white.
tradeoff: The cream tone may feel less at home beside a cool gray interface.

name: Chalk
why: The lightest visual treatment: soft surface, text, and breathing room.
tradeoff: Without a visible border it can blend into similarly light backgrounds.

name: Pearl badge
why: A small status badge separates state from project and message.
tradeoff: The badge and project row add structure beyond the current two-part card.

name: Ivory project
why: The project name becomes the main heading for people juggling several workspaces.
tradeoff: The completion wording is smaller than the project heading.

name: Slim rail
why: A narrow accent rail and reduced height preserve a clear two-part hierarchy.
tradeoff: Only a short message fits before truncation.

name: Compact pill
why: A small rounded capsule works well for short, glanceable updates.
tradeoff: The body is a single line; long messages are intentionally abbreviated.

name: Tight stack
why: Keeps project, state, and message separate in a compact vertical stack.
tradeoff: The extra project row leaves room for only one body line.

name: Inline check
why: A small status symbol anchors a low-height card with strong horizontal alignment.
tradeoff: The symbol column and short height both reduce message space.

name: Mini panel
why: A narrower card saves horizontal space while retaining the familiar hierarchy.
tradeoff: Workspace names and messages wrap sooner.

name: Wide strip
why: A wide, shallow strip favors quick scanning of short updates.
tradeoff: It takes more horizontal space and offers only one body line.

name: Editorial dark
why: A larger project heading makes workspace recognition the first thing you notice.
tradeoff: Long project names need ellipsis even when the message itself is short.

name: Editorial light
why: A quiet, light version of the project-led hierarchy with generous spacing.
tradeoff: The large project heading feels more like a small card than a conventional toast.

name: Mono note
why: A monospace status line and project name give it a precise developer-tool character.
tradeoff: Monospace metadata uses more width and feels more technical.

name: Quiet hierarchy
why: A small status line above a project heading creates a clear, restrained reading order.
tradeoff: The status has less visual emphasis than in the baseline.

name: Footer status
why: The message leads; a quiet footer carries the status after you have read the result.
tradeoff: The completion or attention state is less immediately prominent.

name: Accent typography
why: The title itself carries the accent, leaving the rest of the card completely plain.
tradeoff: The color treatment is subtler than a status icon, especially at a glance.

name: Sage wash
why: A faint sage surface gives the card warmth while keeping the layout familiar.
tradeoff: A colored surface is more of a personal preference than a neutral system look.

name: Blue mist
why: A cool dark surface and fine top line pair naturally with a blue-gray desktop.
tradeoff: The blue accent is an identity color; status is still communicated by the title.

name: Sand
why: Warm neutrals and a text-only layout keep the color treatment understated.
tradeoff: The warmth may clash with a strongly cool or blue desktop.

name: Dusty lilac
why: A desaturated violet surface and small badge add personality without bright colors.
tradeoff: The badge is a stronger styling choice than the baseline dot.

name: Mineral teal
why: A deep teal surface and outlined status symbol feel calm but distinctive.
tradeoff: The icon column makes long messages wrap sooner.

name: Soft silver
why: A slightly lighter dark surface reduces the contrast jump against medium-gray apps.
tradeoff: It has less separation from medium-gray backgrounds than a near-black card.

name: Left rule
why: One thin vertical accent gives a strong visual anchor with very little decoration.
tradeoff: The left accent is more noticeable than a small status dot.

name: Header band
why: A softly tinted header separates status from the message without a hard divider.
tradeoff: Two surface tones give it a more structured appearance.

name: Split surface
why: A small state column keeps the message area visually organized.
tradeoff: The state column takes space from the project and message.

name: Inset message
why: A pale inset groups the message while the status stays in the outer header.
tradeoff: The extra surface makes it a little less spare than the text-only options.

name: Floating check
why: A single softly filled status circle creates a polished focal point.
tradeoff: The larger symbol makes this the most icon-led option.

name: Corner mark
why: Two short corner strokes give the card a recognizable signature without a full accent rail.
tradeoff: The corner treatment is decorative rather than functional.
